newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PM BLASTS PLANS TO OUST HIM.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PM BLASTS PLANS TO OUST HIM.

text.p: Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz on Wednesday lashed out at the junior partner in the ruling leftist coalition, the Peasant Party (PSL), for its plans to dismiss him over government farm policies.

Cimoszewicz, member of ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), said the PSL's motion to hold a parliamentary no-confidence vote against him would hamper the cabinet's urgent work on helping victims of July's catastrophic floods.
"This is tripping up the government in a difficult period, when work should focus on flood relief operations," the prime minister told reporters.
The SLD and opposition parties have dismissed the Peasants' plan as jockeying for electoral advantage before general elections, due on September 21, among its rural electorate.

Peasant leader Waldemar Pawlak said on Tuesday his party's parliamentary caucus would draft a no-confidence motion against Cimoszewicz because the prime minister was delaying a decision to grant farmers advance payments for the 1997 grain harvest.

The no-confidence motion, likely to be voted late in August, has virtually no chances to succeed because the opposition refused to back it and the Peasants alone do not have a simple majority needed to oust Cimoszewicz.
The opposition parties have said it was pointless to dismiss the prime minister just weeks before the elections because voters would soon be able to make their own decision.

The Peasants' would like the government to allow the Agriculture Market Agence (ARR), the food marker regulator, to start doling out advances for farmers, amounting to the value of 45 percent of grains they would later deliver.
The finance ministry said the proposal could prove too costly for the budget if too many farmers fail to deliver the grains, as it happened in 1991.
The ministry has drafted its own plan to help farmers, some of whom now find it hard to sell grains after last year's large imports.
Under the scheme, farmers would get special certificates for grains delivered to selected siloes. The certificates would allow them to seek government-subsidised credits from banks.
Cimoszewicz earlier said week he needed more time and details to decide on the proposals.
